one_liner: Pure-Go embedded LSM key-value store using WiscKey key-value separation; 3.7x lower random-read latency than RocksDB in Dgraph's 2017 test.
what_it_does: Badger is an embeddable, persistent, sorted key-value database for Go programs; it needs no cgo and is the storage engine under Dgraph. You open a directory with badger.Open(options) and do all reads and writes inside MVCC transactions (db.View / db.Update, or NewTransaction plus Commit) that run concurrently with serializable snapshot isolation. It also offers prefix and key-only iterators, TTLs, per-key version access, merge operators, sequences, a WriteBatch bulk-write API, a parallel Stream framework and online backup/restore. It is a different API, not a RocksDB binding or drop-in replacement.
how_it_is_fast: It follows the WiscKey paper (FAST '16): values above ValueThreshold go to an append-only value log that doubles as the write-ahead log, and the LSM tree holds only keys plus 12-byte value pointers (file id, length, offset). This keeps the tree small enough to stay in RAM (Dgraph measured a 1.7 GB LSM tree for 75M keys x 1 KB, against 50 GB for RocksDB), so a point read is an in-memory table search with bloom filters plus one read from the value log. Compactions rewrite only keys and pointers, so write amplification falls as values grow. Supporting pieces are an arena-allocated, atomics-based concurrent skiplist memtable adapted from RocksDB's inline skiplist, per-table bloom filters, Ristretto block and index caches, and mmap-backed value-log files.
when_to_use: Go services that need an embedded, ordered, persistent KV store without cgo. You get plain `go get`, easy cross-compilation, and full visibility in the Go CPU and memory profilers. Cgo pain is why Dgraph replaced its RocksDB binding with Badger.

Random point reads of values around 1 KB or larger, with a dataset bigger than RAM, on local NVMe. The 2017 log shows Get latency 3.7x lower than RocksDB at 128 B, 4.2x lower at 1 KB and 5.4x lower at 16 KB. On current versions this only applies if you lower ValueThreshold so values actually go to the value log.
Bulk loading of large values. In the same log, loading 75M x 1 KB was about 4.6x faster than RocksDB (17m10s vs 78m08s), and 5M x 16 KB about 12x faster (6m55s vs 1h22m21s).
Key-only scans and existence checks. With PrefetchValues=false, iteration never touches the value log: 250M keys took 0.71 s, against 5.8 s for RocksDB's key+value iteration.
Embedded use that needs concurrent ACID transactions with SSI conflict detection, TTLs or multi-version reads. Dgraph, Jaeger and go-ipfs are listed users.
when_not_to_use: Small values under write-heavy load. In the same log Badger loaded 250M x 128 B more slowly than RocksDB (45m27s vs 39m11s) and 1B x 16 B about 1.9x more slowly (3h04m vs 1h38m). Dgraph's blog blames Badger's slower compactions.

Range scans that return values. Iterating 250M x 128 B with values took 75.8 s vs 5.8 s for RocksDB (about 13x slower), and about 4x slower at 1 KB, because each value is a separate read from the value log.

Memory-limited or 32-bit deployments. Peak RSS while loading was about 14 GB vs 0.6 GB for RocksDB. Value-log files are always mmapped, since the FileIO mode was removed in v3. Users report page-cache thrashing in 500 MB containers (#2255) and mmap failures on 386 (#2287).

Heavy delete or overwrite workloads that need disk space back automatically. The application has to drive value-log GC through RunValueLogGC, which frees at most one file per call. Open issues report GC stalls when the active file has the most garbage (#2334) and tombstones that automatic compaction never removes from L6 (#2329).

Non-Go stacks, or anything that expects RocksDB's API, on-disk format or tools. Badger's own on-disk format also changes between major versions, and moving data across one requires a backup and restore.

integration.dependencies: Pure Go, no cgo. Depends on dgraph-io/ristretto/v2 (caches and allocator), klauspost/compress (zstd), cespare/xxhash, google/flatbuffers, protobuf, golang.org/x/sys, OpenTelemetry (zpages) and cobra (CLI only). jemalloc is optional: only the CLI Makefile builds with the `jemalloc` tag.
integration.min_toolchain: go.mod declares go 1.24.0, though the README still says Go 1.23+. Import path is github.com/dgraph-io/badger/v4.
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS and BSD are fully supported (POSIX locking and fsync). On Windows, directory locking works differently. AIX has no directory fsync, and Plan9 and WASM/JS have no file locking. 32-bit builds are fragile because of mmap address-space limits (#2287), and a ppc64el test failure is open (#2079). The source tree contains no assembly files.
integration.thread_safety: The DB is safe for concurrent use, and many transactions can run at once, with SSI conflict detection returning ErrConflict on commit. A single Txn is not thread-safe, so call its methods serially. A directory lock allows one read-write process per directory; ReadOnly mode lets several processes open the same directory.

gotchas: Current defaults do not match the benchmark. Since v3.2103.0 (2021), ValueThreshold defaults to 1 MB, so values under 1 MB are stored inline in the LSM tree and Badger behaves like an ordinary LSM store. The default was 32 B until it was raised to 1 KB and then 1 MB. The 2017 run also used TableLoadingMode=LoadToRAM, an option removed in v3.2011.0. Call WithValueThreshold with a small value to get the WiscKey behaviour that was measured.

Space reclamation is manual. Call db.RunValueLogGC(ratio) on a ticker, re-running while it returns nil. It never collects inline values or the active vlog file. TTL expiry and deletes also do not shrink a database that has stopped taking writes, because compactions only run when writes arrive.

Use v4.9.6 or later. v4.9.3 and v4.9.4 fixed deleted keys reappearing after compaction (#2278) and after vlog GC (#2310), and fixed acknowledged writes being dropped during DropPrefix/DropAll (#2313). The v4.9.4 compaction fix then slowed large bulk imports about 3x (#2327), which v4.9.6 fixed (#2330).

Transaction and size limits: a transaction fails with ErrTxnTooBig once pending writes pass 15% of MemTableSize (use WriteBatch for bulk loads). Keys are capped at 65,000 bytes and values at ValueLogFileSize. Calling Close twice, or writing after Close, panics with a closed-channel error.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Badger when the application is written in Go and must stay cgo-free: every catalogued sibling (Titan, PebblesDB, SplinterDB, NuDB, ToplingDB, etc.) is C/C++. If you already run RocksDB and want the same key-value-separation gain for large values, Titan provides it as a RocksDB plugin (reported ~70% faster data loading) without changing engine or API.
verified_claims_summary: Dgraph ran this benchmark itself in 2017 on a 2-core AWS i3.large (16 GB RAM, local NVMe, ~93K 4 KB random-read IOPS). Random Gets over 250M 22-byte keys with 128 B values averaged 32.4 us in Badger vs 119.0 us in RocksDB 5.1.4 called through cgo (3.67x), and loading 75M x 1 KB took 17m10s vs 78m08s (~4.6x). RocksDB was opened read-only with its default block cache and a 16-bit bloom filter while Badger held its LSM tables in RAM (LoadToRAM), and neither the Go version nor the CPU model is stated.
status_note: Actively maintained (v4.9.6 released 2026-08-05, commits through 2026-09-21), Apache-2.0, and used in production by Dgraph, Jaeger and go-ipfs. The headline numbers, though, come from an archived 2017 benchmark whose options and defaults no longer exist, so re-benchmark current v4 before relying on them.
